questions.prompt: A short story tells how a proud eagle laughs at a slow tortoise, loses a race to it, and admits at the close that patience had beaten speed. The last line prints that lesson for the reader. What kind of narrative is it?

options.text: a myth: gods, and the beginning of the world or of a custom
a slice of life: one ordinary moment of ordinary living
a fable: animals who behave like people, and a moral at the end
a historical narrative: real people and real events of the past

questions.explanation: Two signatures identify a fable and this story carries both: the characters are animals who talk and reason exactly as people do, and the lesson is printed for you in the closing line instead of being left to you. A myth would explain how something in the world came to exist, and gods would be in it. A historical narrative would be tied to people who really lived and to events that really happened, which no race between an eagle and a tortoise ever was. And a slice of life takes one ordinary moment of ordinary living and finds no marvel in it at all, whereas talking animals are a marvel from the first sentence.

questions.prompt: The old queen's cough grew worse through the night, and before dawn her son sent for the palace physician. Where is the physician a few minutes later?

options.text: on his way to the palace, because he has been called there
at his own house, reading a letter that has only just arrived
in the palace kitchen, where he has been living all week
outside the city, because the son has dismissed him

questions.explanation: To send for someone is not to send that person anything: it is to call them to you and expect them to come. The only thing that travels outwards is the message, and the person travels back. That is why the physician is on the road to the palace. Reading a letter would be right if the son had written to him instead of summoning him, and writing is precisely what this expression does not describe. Living in the kitchen makes the summons pointless, since a man already in the building need not be sent for. And dismissing him reverses the direction: sending someone away is the opposite of sending for them.

questions.prompt: A tale opens with this sentence: "The night was so dark that the shepherd lost the path he had walked for twenty years." What is the sentence telling you?

options.text: Losing the path is what made the night seem dark to him.
The darkness of the night is what made him lose the path.
The night was dark, and he lost the path as well, by chance.
The night was dark, and yet he managed to keep to the path.

questions.explanation: This pattern always runs one way. The first half measures something — not merely dark, dark to a degree — and the half after that reports what that degree brought about. The darkness therefore comes first and the lost path follows from it. Reversing the two makes the shepherd's mistake the cause of the weather, which no sentence of this shape can mean. Reading them as two separate facts throws away the whole point of the pattern, which exists precisely to tie them. And nothing here is a contrast: had the shepherd kept to his path, the sentence would have needed a word such as "although".

questions.prompt: Here is a whole story in four sentences. "Every morning the women of the village filled their jars at the old well. One July night the well ran dry. For a week the families argued about whose new orchard had drunk the water. In the end they dug a second well together and shared it." Which moment is the problem — the one event without which there would be no story at all?

options.text: the women filling their jars there each morning
the families arguing for a week over the orchard
the digging of a second well by the two sides
the July night on which the old well gave out

questions.explanation: The problem is the single occasion that breaks a state of affairs which had been holding until then, and the text marks it with a date: one July night. Notice how the opening sentence is built by comparison — every morning, a habit with no date, nothing going wrong — which is the mark of an introduction and never of a problem. The week of arguing comes after the break and belongs to the episodes that develop it. And digging together is how the trouble is settled, which makes it the resolution: it closes the story instead of opening it.

questions.prompt: A chronicler records that the king's treasurer behaved shamefully at the banquet. What is he telling us?

options.text: that the treasurer was far too shy to say a word all evening
that the treasurer acted in a way that brought him disgrace
that the treasurer was ashamed of the food he was served
that the treasurer behaved better than anyone had hoped

questions.explanation: The adverb judges the conduct: to act shamefully is to act in a way that brings disgrace on the one who acts, and it is the chronicler, not the treasurer, who is passing that judgement. The two traps are close relatives of the word and neither will do. Being shy is a difficulty in speaking and carries no disgrace at all; being ashamed is a feeling inside the person, which may follow the conduct but is not the conduct itself — a man can behave shamefully and feel nothing. As for behaving better than expected, that reverses the judgement completely.
